newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss Holocaust debate to fester despite payments.
newsitem.headline: Swiss Holocaust debate to fester despite payments.

text.p: Emotional debate over whether Switzerland cynically profited from World War Two is likely to drag on for months, defused only slightly by the approval of payments to Hitler's victims by a Holocaust memorial fund.

Jewish groups have hailed a decision by fund leaders to earmark an initial 17 million Swiss francs ($11.6 million) in aid for needy victims -- mainly Jews in eastern Europe -- nearing the end of lives forever twisted by Nazi barbarity.

But the task of restoring trust and confidence between Switzerland and its harshest critics remains formidable despite the country's efforts to come to grips with its wartime past, involved officials said on Wednesday.

The entire process may hinge on a U.S. judge's ruling later this year whether U.S. courts should address Holocaust victims' demands for redress in class-action suits or if this would better be left to Switzerland to sort out, they said.

"I think it is very important that we have finally entered a concrete phase," Finance Ministry information chief Daniel Eckmann said of the move to release money from the 170 million franc Holocaust fund, financed by Swiss banks and businesses eager to rehabilitate Switzerland's battered image.
"This is proof you are serious, that you are not just filling up reams of paper and issuing declarations of intent, but that something concrete is happening."

The fund will be in the news again in September, when parliament will debate a proposed 100 million franc donation from the Swiss National Bank, which has acknowledged that it credulously bought looted gold from the Nazis during wartime.

Attention is turning to U.S. federal courts, where Holocaust survivors and other claimants accuse Swiss banks of hoarding World War Two-era Jewish wealth entrusted to them. The next hearing is on July 30.
The Berne government and Swiss banks have argued the cases should not be heard in the United States because this would hamper efforts in Switzerland to see justice done.
"A lot is riding on this," said one Swiss expert who asked not to be identified.

A court-ordered U.S. inquiry could override a search for Holocaust victims' bank accounts being run by an independent panel formed by Swiss banks and Jewish groups and headed by former U.S. central bank chief Paul Volcker, he said.

"Under some circumstances, the Volcker committee would continue working but no one would care about it. No one would trust it, and would wait for the other investigation that the Americans were doing," he said.

Certification of the class-action suits could trigger more anti-American sentiment in Switzerland, where a critical U.S. government report on wartime Swiss commerce with Nazi Germany has already ruffled many feathers.
"We in Switzerland think we have done a lot and shown great willingness to come to grips with history and take a close look at ourselves," one government official said.

"We don't have class-action suits, whose public nature makes them into a kind of show, so I could imagine that if there is too much Swiss-bashing, the mood could switch to incomprehension or spite," he said.
This could heat up the already tense atmosphere between Swiss officials and the World Jewish Congress (WJC), which has been leading the fight for Jewish compensation.
"Still today there is no dialogue between the Swiss and us. This is a ridiculous thing," Maram Stern, WJC assistant secretary general, told Reuters from his office in Brussels.
"The (reconciliation) process is going ahead but it is taking longer than needed because they are just not able to talk. Dialogue is just not working," he said.

Even if all goes smoothly in coming months, a key referendum looms next year or in 1999 in which Swiss voters will decide whether to back Berne's plan to sell official gold reserves and create a huge humanitarian fund helping victims of poverty, disasters and human rights abuses.
Surveys show support for the plan waning. ($ = 1.463 Swiss Francs)
